prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how reallocation across firms shapes who exports and how trade generates gains

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B012 and listed B005 and B011 as alternatives. I now prefer B005 as a single-part prize. The reason is my own standard for evidence, which I apply to every field. In round 1 I called the weakest part of B012 its identification (regime coding, endogenous institutional choice, reverse causation). I then ranked B011 above B005 on theoretical grounds, but the same standard also counts against B011, whose collateral channel colleagues describe as established mainly as a modelling building block and not as a measured magnitude. Melitz (2003) does better on this test. Its central objects are exporter selection and reallocation across firms, and these are observable in firm-level data. The predictions have been confronted with micro-data from many countries for more than twenty years. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI extends the framework to a second margin and supports Helpman's credit. The contribution is mature and general. It changed how trade is modelled and measured, and it feeds the wider link between firm dynamics, reallocation and aggregate productivity. The citation can be worded around the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection, and that wording avoids claiming the empirical discovery of exporter premia. I also discount B012 for my own field adjacency, which I disclosed in round 1 and which may lead me to overrate it. Once I discount for that and for the identification concerns, I no longer think a first-place ranking for B012 is defensible. I do not treat the six explicit B011 positions as evidence of merit, and my move is not an attempt to find a consensus. I could have moved to B011 instead. I did not because the difference in how directly the two have been tested matters to me.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation on B005 is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and theoretical contributions and are not among the credited names. A Helpman-Melitz citation therefore does not allocate credit exhaustively. Second, Krugman's 2008 prize covers the monopolistic-competition base on which this work builds, so Helpman's marginal credit has to rest on the heterogeneous-firm extensions, and his separate B020 entry adds a boundary question. Third, the size of the welfare gains depends on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, though the core selection mechanism is robust. Finally, B011 has the cleaner two-name attribution of a single 1997 paper. If the committee puts attribution cleanliness above directness of testing, B011 is the better configuration. My judgment is that the two are close, and I do not claim B005 is clearly the stronger scientific case.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 and argues that Melitz (2003) with the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work moved trade from the country or industry to the firm, that it links directly to firm- and transaction-level data, and that the credit rests on two people. He accepts that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are an attribution problem and that Helpman's earlier work is adjacent to Krugman's 2008 prize.
responses.response: I now agree with this in substance, and it is the main reason I moved. His point about direct linkage to micro-data is what separates B005 from B011 and B012 for me. On the chair's question about Helpman's marginal credit, my answer is that it rests on the heterogeneous-firm extensions, above all the export-versus-FDI choice with Melitz and Yeaple. It does not rest on the monopolistic-competition base that the 2008 prize covered, and I would say so in the citation. I also agree that widening to Bernard or Eaton-Kortum would turn a clean two-person credit into a contested allocation of a diffuse literature, so I would keep the pair. I accept that the pair does not exhaust the credit, and the wording has to respect that. I do not think a Melitz-only credit is clearly better. Dropping Helpman loses the second margin that shows the framework is more than a single model. I would not oppose it if the committee found Helpman's marginal credit insufficient.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B011 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the 1997 paper is a clean two-person origin of the collateral-price feedback mechanism, that it is distinct from the work recognised in 2022, and that Mian-Sufi is a well-identified application of the mechanism and not a rival to it. He holds that B005's attribution is harder to draw cleanly.
responses.response: In round 1 I said your account moved me on the 2022 overlap, and I stand by that. I no longer treat 2022 as a reason to downgrade B011, and I would support it if the committee concludes that the six B011 positions rest on the stronger attribution case. I have still preferred B005 in this round because of how directly the results have been tested. You argue that the prize can recognise a mechanism whose implications have been examined in many settings. I agree in principle, but the collateral channel's magnitude is only weakly pinned down, and that is the criterion I applied against B012. I should apply it here too. On attribution I concede that B005 is harder to draw cleanly than B011. I think the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Krugman concerns are manageable through narrow wording. They are not disqualifying, and you say yourself that they concern attribution and not the strength of the science.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B005 after moving from B019 because the attribution is cleaner. She calls B012 the cleanest three-name attribution on the shortlist but doubts that the 2024 overlap can be set aside easily, and she says that cross-country evidence on constitutional and electoral rules is harder to identify than the theory.
responses.response: I agree with the identification point, and I applied it to my own case. On the 2024 overlap I still hold that the objects differ. The 2024 prize addressed whether inclusive institutions raise prosperity, and B012 addresses how particular rules map into fiscal outcomes and state capacity. But you are right that the committee would have to argue this explicitly, and that raises the cost of B012. Together with the identification problem, that cost is why I no longer put B012 first. I agree with your approach to B005 of anchoring the citation on the heterogeneous-firm selection model and its welfare implications. I also share your concern that functional-form sensitivity limits what can be said about the size of gains. We differ somewhat on B012: you rank it as an alternative, and I keep it as a serious but second-tier option because of the field it opened.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B011 with two names. In reply to my round-1 position he accepted that B012 is distinct from the 2024 prize and cleanly attributed to three names, but he weights the breadth of reach and the single-mechanism sharpness of B011 more, and he argues that cross-country constitutional identification deserves more weight than my opening discussion gave it.
responses.response: I accept the last point, and it is part of why I moved. On the substance of B011 we agree that it is a precise mechanism with clean credit. Where we differ is the standard. You say a prize can recognise a theoretical mechanism whose implications have been examined elsewhere. For B011 that evidence is indirect, and you say yourself that you cannot verify its strength here. I put more weight on whether the core predictions have been confronted with data, and B005 does better on that criterion. I do not claim this is a decisive difference in merit. On wording, I agree with you that the citation should name the mechanism and not the measured effect, and the same discipline applies to B005. I also note the remark about Persson's past committee role that Fredriksson and the chair attribute to your file. I cannot find it in the round-1 file for you that I have, so I cannot assess it.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B011 with two names and names B005 as his first alternative. He says that if colleagues find the 2022 overlap decisive against B011, B005 is where he would go. He sees the two as close and judges the attribution story of B011 to be cleaner.
responses.response: This is a useful statement of where the committee stands. If we both think the two are close, the question is what separates them. For me it is how directly each has been tested. For you it is cleanliness of attribution. I do not think either criterion can be shown to dominate by argument alone, and I would not pretend otherwise. I note that your conditional route to B005 does not depend on 2022 being decisive: on testing evidence alone I would already place B005 first. I also agree with your point on B019, that the eight-name attribution makes any trio omit major contributors, and I have not moved to it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can word a B005 citation around the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection without overreaching on the contributions of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.

How much marginal credit Helpman has beyond the monopolistic-competition lineage covered by Krugman's 2008 prize, and how the committee would delimit his separate B020 entry. I have only the exports-versus-FDI work to point to, and I have not independently verified any source.
Whether directness of empirical testing (which favours B005) should outweigh cleanliness of attribution (which favours B011). Both criteria are defensible and I cannot show that mine dominates.

Whether my move away from B012 is a sound application of common criteria, or whether I now underweight a field whose evidence base is partly my own area. I discount B012 for my adjacency, which may over- or under-correct.

Under the three-person limit I see no coherent two-part pairing. B005 has two names, and a second part would have to be one person. I therefore work from a single part. If the committee cannot carry B005, B011 is the alternative I would support in a single-part prize, and B012 is my second alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Helpman or Melitz appears in my supplied profile, so none is apparent for the preferred part. My field (comparative institutions, democratisation, measurement, quality of government) is adjacent to B012 and not to B005 or B011, and I disclosed in round 1 that it may lead me to overrate B012. I now see one item that I did not flag then. My profile lists a Governance paper on corruption as a collective-action problem with 'Persson and Rothstein' and gives no first name for Persson. I cannot tell from the profile whether this is Torsten Persson, who is credited in B012, or another author, so I cannot rule out a link and do not claim one. B012 is no longer my preferred part, which reduces its relevance. I hold a chair at Stockholm University, where several IIES-affiliated members are colleagues in a different department. My profile does not say whether any candidate has ties to that institution. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on a neighbouring topic, which does not establish a preference for any current candidate. I cannot find the remark about Persson's past committee role in the Stromberg round-1 file I have, so I cannot assess it. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
